become overly compliant when feeling threatened
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I remember the event I feel intense rage

I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a male torture survivor, sexual-trauma-specific verbal cues are possible only if sexual torture or sexual humiliation is part of the trauma, but the rest of the profile provides no corresponding sexual content in memory, appraisals, threat, or coping. As selected, this trigger appears disconnected from the trauma representation and is hard to justify clinically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him implies shame/marked visible contamination or exposure. That could occur after torture, but here it is not supported by the memory items, trigger content, or other appraisals, making it feel mismatched with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is poorly linked to the active formulation. The main connected pattern is triggers ↔ negative appraisals with memory-linked re-experiencing and threat-driven compliance/detachment. Gambling introduces a separate excitement-seeking coping style that is not reflected elsewhere and feels clinically disconnected rather than integrated.

vignette: Seventy-year-old widower Carlos still wakes up with a start most nights, his heart racing like it did on that fateful evening when the military stormed into their small village. The screams of the women and children still echo in his mind as if it were yesterday. He remembers trying to shield his wife from the chaos, but being dragged away, beaten, and left for dead. Carlos doesn't recall much of what happened next; he only knows that when he came to, he was alone, battered, and confused. The nightmares persisted even after Carlos fled to America, rebuilt a life as a welder, and raised two children with his wife, Maria. He thought time would dull the memories, but they remain seared into his mind like hot metal. Now, whenever Carlos hears the sound of gunfire or fireworks, he is instantly transported back to that night, reliving every moment of terror and helplessness. His palms grow sweaty, and he can't shake off the feeling of being trapped with no options for escape. As a coping mechanism, Carlos often detaches himself from these memories, observing them as if they belong to someone else. But when the emotions overwhelm him, his anger boils over, and he feels like he's reliving the rage all over again. He struggles to articulate what happened that night; words get stuck in his throat, and the narrative falters. It's as if his mind is trying to safeguard itself from revisiting those moments of raw terror. Carlos has always been a proud man, but the experience left him with an unshakeable fear that he can never truly trust anyone – even himself. He often wonders whether he should have done more to prevent what happened or fought back harder. The weight of these questions haunts him still, and on some days, it's hard for Carlos to find meaning in anything. Since Maria passed away a few years ago, the silence has become oppressive. Carlos tries to fill the void by being overly accommodating with friends and family, hoping that if he just gives enough, they'll stay close and keep him safe. But deep down, he feels like he's living on borrowed time, always waiting for another shoe to drop. Lately, even simple tasks have become arduous. Carlos used to take pride in his work as a welder, but the sound of metal screeching or sparks flying makes him jump now. His employers are growing impatient with his lack of focus, and coworkers whisper about his declining skills behind his back. Carlos tries hard not to think about the past, but the memories keep creeping up on him like shadows in the night. His children have encouraged him to seek help, worried that their once-resilient father is losing himself to these ghosts from the past. For the first time in decades, Carlos has begun questioning whether he can ever truly be free of what happened all those years ago. He's starting to wonder if it's possible to forgive himself and learn to live with the memories rather than trying to outrun them. With a mix of trepidation and hope, Carlos is taking his first tentative steps toward facing these demons head-on, uncertain about what lies ahead but knowing he can't stay trapped forever.
